The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions that either keep almost every vector (undoing the computational savings) or compress too aggressively and discard essential information; it acts like a load‑balancing regularizer that steers the network toward a desired compression level [S1].  
In the loss formulation, F is defined as the fraction of vectors that are actually selected by the routing module (i.e., the average of the binary selection indicators b_t) [S1].  
 G is the average boundary probability output by the routing module (the mean of the probabilities p_t) [S1].  
 N is a scalar that sets the target compression ratio for the stage, controlling how many vectors should be retained relative to the input length [S1].  
Because F is nondifferentiable, the model is trained to match G to F, allowing gradient‑based optimization to achieve the intended compression ratio specified by N [S1].  
When F equals G, the ratio loss attains its minimum value of 1 at the target ratio F = G = 1/N, effectively guiding the model toward that compression goal in practice [S1].

record.text: Inner Monologue is a method in Moshi that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens while remaining compatible with streaming inference, enabling the model to treat speech and text as interleaved streams [S3]. This single delay hyper‑parameter enables switching between ASR and TTS with no changes to loss, architecture, or training data, demonstrating the flexibility of Inner Monologue for real‑time speech applications [S1][S2][S3].

The Transformer adds a “positional encoding” vector to each token embedding, where each encoding has the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) as the word embeddings and is computed with sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies: \(PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) and \(PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) so that each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid whose wavelength forms a geometric progression [S1].  
These sinusoidal encodings can be summed with the token embeddings because they share the same dimensionality [S1].  
The authors hypothesized that such functions make it easy for the model to learn relative positions, since any fixed offset \(k\) yields a linear relationship between \(PE_{pos+k}\) and \(PE_{pos}\) [S1].  
They also found experimentally that replacing the sinusoidal version with learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical translation quality, but retained the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training [S1][S2].

Scaled dot‑product attention takes a query vector and a set of key‑value pairs, computes the dot product between the query and each key to measure similarity, and then uses those scores (after a softmax) as weights to form a weighted sum of the corresponding values [S2].  
Before applying the softmax, each dot product is divided by the square root of the key dimension \( \sqrt{d_k}\) to keep the magnitude of the scores moderate [S1].  
The scaling prevents the raw dot products from becoming large when \(d_k\) is big, which would push the softmax into regions with very small gradients and hinder learning [S1].

record.text:
H‑Net determines chunk boundaries with a learned routing module that evaluates each byte’s contextual representation and outputs a binary indicator bₜ for whether a cut should be placed at that position [S2].  
During training the model receives gradients through a straight‑through estimator, allowing it to discover data‑dependent segmentation strategies without any external heuristics [S2].  
Empirically, the learned boundaries tend to align with natural linguistic delimiters such as whitespace, because the model discovers that word boundaries are semantically meaningful units [S3].  
However, the routing decisions are not fixed to whitespace; the module also merges or splits tokens based on surrounding content, creating chunks that span multiple words or that begin at the first characters of words when that improves predictability [S3].  
When whitespace is removed, H‑Net still places cuts at semantically relevant points, showing that its decisions depend on both the byte values and the broader context rather than simple static rules [S3].  
Thus, H‑Net decides where to cut by jointly learning a context‑aware boundary predictor that outputs binary cut signals, guided by end‑to‑end training objectives and reinforced by observed content‑aware patterns such as whitespace and word‑initial characters [S2][S3].

H‑Net determines chunk boundaries with a learned routing module that uses the current contextual representation of each byte to produce a binary indicator bₜ signaling whether a cut should be placed at that position [S2].  
During training the routing module is optimized jointly with the downstream language model, so the boundary decisions become data‑dependent and are shaped by the task loss rather than any handcrafted heuristic [S2].  
Empirically, a single‑stage H‑Net learns to place most cuts at whitespace characters, effectively treating word boundaries as natural segmentation points [S3].  
In a two‑stage hierarchy, the first stage still focuses on spacelike bytes but additionally marks the first few characters of each word, allowing the model to capture the predictable remainder of the word [S3].  
Beyond these simple patterns, H‑Net also merges multiple words or inserts cuts based on richer semantic content and surrounding context, showing that its decisions are content‑aware rather than fixed to static byte values [S3].  
Thus, H‑Net decides where to cut the byte stream by jointly learning a context‑driven routing signal that typically aligns with linguistic delimiters yet adapts to broader semantic cues.

record.text: Inner Monologue is a method that interleaves text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, letting the model predict speech on a per‑frame basis rather than waiting for an entire transcript before generating audio [S3]. By inserting a fixed delay between the two token streams, the same Moshi model can be repurposed for streaming tasks: delaying audio tokens by about 2 seconds gives the model a look‑ahead on text and enables a streaming TTS system, while delaying text tokens by the same amount lets the model listen to audio before emitting text, yielding a streaming ASR system [S1][S2]. In streaming TTS the model is teacher‑forced on the text tokens at inference and generates audio with a temperature of 0.6, whereas in streaming ASR the audio tokens are teacher‑forced and the model decodes text greedily [S1]. This simple change of delay therefore provides both low‑latency speech synthesis and recognition without training separate models [S1][S2].

The positional encodings are added to the token embeddings at the bottom of both encoder and decoder and have the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) so they can be summed element‑wise [S1].  
Each encoding dimension is defined by a sinusoid: for even indices \(2i\) the value is \(\sin(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) and for odd indices \(2i+1\) it is \(\cos(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\), yielding a set of frequencies that form a geometric progression from \(2\pi\) to \(10000\cdot2\pi\) [S1].  
The authors hypothesized that these sinusoids let the model easily learn relative positions, because any fixed offset \(k\) produces a linear relationship between \(PE_{pos+k}\) and \(PE_{pos}\) [S1].  
They also tried learned positional embeddings and obtained nearly identical translation quality, but chose the sinusoidal form because it can extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than seen during training [S1][S2].

record.text: Inner Monologue is the component of Moshi that aligns text tokens with audio tokens by inserting padding tokens (EPAD) and allowing a configurable delay between the two modalities, so that the language model can decide which stream leads the other during generation [S2]. By setting a positive delay for the audio tokens (e.g., delaying audio by 2 seconds), the model can listen to upcoming audio before generating text, and during inference the audio tokens are forced to the ground‑truth while only text tokens are sampled, yielding a streaming automatic‑speech‑recognition system that also provides fine‑grained word‑level alignments [S1][S2]. Conversely, by delaying the text tokens (e.g., delaying text by 2 seconds) the model generates audio conditioned on already‑available text, and at inference the text tokens are forced while only audio tokens are sampled, producing a streaming text‑to‑speech system [S1][S2]. The same single Moshi model and loss function are used for both tasks; only the delay hyper‑parameter is changed to switch between ASR and TTS [S1][S2].

record.text: Inner Monologue is a design in Moshi that aligns text tokens with audio tokens in a streaming hierarchical sequence, allowing the same model to be used for both ASR and TTS by adjusting the delay between modalities [S1][S2]. By delaying audio tokens by 2 seconds relative to text tokens, the model samples text conditioned on previously generated audio, creating a streaming TTS system that generates speech in real time while maintaining 0.6 temperature decoding [S1]. Conversely, delaying text tokens by 2 seconds lets the model listen to audio before emitting text, yielding a streaming ASR system that performs greedy decoding and produces word‑level alignments with 80 ms precision [S1][S2]. The same single delay hyper‑parameter can switch the system from ASR to TTS without any changes to loss, architecture, or training data, demonstrating flexibility in the Inner Monologue framework [S2]. Moshi’s overall architecture combines a Helium text language model, a Mimi‑distilled audio codec, and the Inner Monologue delay mechanism to support full‑duplex dialogue with semantic and acoustic token streams [S3]. Thus, Inner Monologue enables Moshi to cast both streaming ASR and TTS as different instantiations of a unified multimodal language model.

record.text: Moshi is engineered as a multi‑stream speech‑to‑speech Transformer that can simultaneously encode the user’s audio stream, decode its own audio output, and produce text tokens in one forward pass, enabling full‑duplex dialogue without explicit turn boundaries [S2]. The architecture employs separate input and output audio streams that feed into a Depth Transformer capable of streaming inference, so that new user frames can be processed while the model continues generating its own speech frames [S2]. By jointly modeling text and audio tokens through the Inner Monologue procedure, Moshi preserves paralinguistic information and reduces the need for an external ASR, allowing the model to respond as soon as it receives speech rather than waiting for a full turn [S1][S2]. The neural audio codec Mimi merges semantic and acoustic features into a single tokenizer, which keeps the output audio high‑quality and computationally efficient even when both streams are active [S2]. Because the model processes both streams in parallel and does not enforce strict speaker‑turn segmentation, it can handle overlapping speech from the user and its own output, thereby supporting real‑time, full‑duplex communication [S2].
